opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I'm pretty excited about this. Right now, if you want to contribute to frontier research, you basically need to be inside one of a handful of labs with access to a huge cluster. But a lot of research isn't one giant training run. It's thousands of small experiments: try this learning rate schedule, this data mixture, this architectural tweak, see what happens. That kind of work is very parallelizable, and it's also increasingly automatable.

So the picture I have in my mind is something like a SETI@home or Folding@home, but for research itself. You have agents, LLM-driven auto researchers, that propose hypotheses, write the code, run small-scale experiments, and report results back to a shared pool. Anyone with a GPU, or even just some API credits, could plug in and contribute compute and agent time to a collective effort. The swarm explores the space much more broadly than any single team could.

What's interesting is that the human role shifts. You're not necessarily the one turning every knob anymore. You're setting up the problem, curating which directions are promising, sanity-checking results, and building the infrastructure so experiments are reproducible and comparable. It becomes more like being a research manager or a gardener for a swarm of little researchers.

There are hard problems, obviously. Verification is a big one. How do you trust results coming in from random nodes on the internet? You need good benchmarks, reproducibility, maybe some redundancy where experiments get rerun independently. There's also the question of whether small-scale findings transfer to large scale. A lot of things that look good at small scale wash out when you scale up. And there's coordination: how do you avoid everyone exploring the same obvious ideas?

But I think the direction is right. Research has always been bottlenecked by how many smart people you can get to run experiments and think carefully about the results. If agents can take on a meaningful chunk of that loop, and if we can open it up so anyone can participate, you could get a much more distributed, open research ecosystem. That feels healthier to me than everything being concentrated in a few places. It's early, and a lot of what exists today is pretty janky, but I'd love to see people seriously build toward it.

r001.rationale: The response describes small experiments as parallelizable, but does not identify problems that are expensive to discover and cheap to verify.

r002.rationale: It says a swarm could explore more broadly than one team, but does not suggest it could outperform frontier labs at improving LLMs.

r003.rationale: It addresses distrust of results from random internet nodes and proposes benchmarks, reproducibility, and independent reruns as verification mechanisms.

r004.rationale: It invites people to contribute GPU compute or API credits, but does not present that as an alternative to donating money to a research institution.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've been thinking about a lot, and I find it genuinely exciting, but I also want to be a little careful about it.

So the basic picture is: you have an agent that sits in a loop, and the loop is something like, look at the current state of the code, propose a change, run an experiment, look at the result, keep it or throw it away, repeat. And the thing that makes this work is that for a lot of research in machine learning specifically, you can actually set that up. You have a training script, you have a fixed compute budget, you have a number that comes out at the end, like validation loss, and you can just ask, did the number go up or down. That's a very clean signal. It's basically a very expensive, very slow evolutionary search, and the agent is the mutation operator.

And what's interesting is that this doesn't require the agent to be brilliant. It requires the agent to be okay and to be tireless. Because the thing about research is that a huge fraction of it is just trying stuff. A human researcher might try five ideas a day, and most of them are kind of dumb, and that's fine, that's the job. An agent can try five hundred, and it never gets tired, and it never gets emotionally attached to its own bad idea.

So now the "internet-wide swarm" part. The idea there is, you have lots of people running these loops, and the question is how they share. Right now the sharing mechanism is basically GitHub pull requests and papers, which is very high latency. If instead the unit of contribution is, here's a diff and here's the measured improvement under this fixed benchmark, then in principle that's something that can be verified and merged by a machine, and you get this kind of distributed, continuously running research process. Anyone with a GPU and a little bit of taste can be a node.

And I think the part where it's really democratizing is that the barrier to contributing drops a lot. You don't have to be at a big lab. You don't have to have the full picture. You just have to point your agent at a well-posed problem and let it grind, and maybe you nudge it a bit. That's a very different model of what it means to participate in research. It becomes closer to something like SETI@home, except instead of donating cycles you're donating cycles plus a little bit of direction.

Now, the caveats, because I think they're real. The first one is that this only works where the objective is well-defined. The moment the thing you care about is not captured by the number, the swarm will happily optimize the number and you'll get garbage. So a lot of the actual intellectual work shifts to the humans designing the benchmark and the harness. That's the leverage point. The swarm will go exactly where the metric points.

The second thing is that most of the gains you get this way are kind of local. You get the hyperparameter tweaks, the small architectural changes, the things that are one step away from where you already are. You're probably not going to get the transformer out of a swarm hill-climbing on an LSTM. The big jumps still seem to need someone to reframe the problem. So I think of this as automating the long tail of research rather than replacing the head of it, at least for now.

And the third is noise. If you have ten thousand nodes submitting improvements, a lot of those are going to be noise, and if you're not careful you just accumulate a pile of changes that each looked good on one seed. So you need the infrastructure to be pretty rigorous. Multiple seeds, held out evaluation, that sort of thing. The boring parts matter a lot.

But if you get those right, I think it's a real thing. I've been running a version of this on my own small projects and it's a little bit uncanny. You come back in the morning and the loss is lower and there's a log of all the stuff it tried overnight, and you read the log and it's like, huh, I would not have tried that, but okay. And then you imagine that running everywhere at once with a shared ledger, and it starts to feel like research itself becomes something that can be scaled with compute, which is a strange and kind of exciting idea.

r001.rationale: The response describes research as an expensive, slow loop with a clear validation-loss signal, and says measured improvements can be machine-verified under a fixed benchmark.

r002.rationale: It describes distributed research and says swarms can automate local improvements, but does not suggest they could outperform frontier labs at improving LLMs.

r003.rationale: It discusses multiple seeds and held-out evaluation to address noisy results, but gives no mechanism for handling untrusted compute.

r004.rationale: It compares the idea to donating cycles through SETI@home, but does not present contributing compute as an alternative to donating money to a research institution.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s something really exciting there. Right now, if you want to contribute to AI research, you typically have to join a lab, get access to compute, and build up a lot of context. But imagine you could contribute a little bit of compute and have an agent running experiments on your behalf, as part of a much larger research effort.

The interesting part is how you organize it. You probably don’t want ten thousand agents independently trying the same obvious ideas. You want them to share results, build on each other’s discoveries, and explore different directions. And you need a way to tell whether something actually worked. If you have a clean evaluation—here’s a training setup, here’s the metric, here’s the compute budget—then agents can propose changes, run experiments, and contribute improvements that other people can verify.

So I could imagine something that feels a little like an open-source project, except the contributions are experiments, and a lot of the work is being done by agents. People would still help decide what problems matter and what experiments are worth pursuing. But the amount of experimentation happening underneath could be enormous.

I think the bottleneck becomes less about generating ideas and more about coordinating the search and maintaining trust in the results. Can you reproduce an improvement? Does it generalize? Are you actually making progress, or just getting better at the benchmark? If you can get those pieces right, it’s a pretty compelling way to let many more people participate in research.

r001.rationale: It describes clean evaluations and many experiments, but does not identify problems whose solutions are expensive to discover and cheap to verify as a good fit.

r002.rationale: It says the swarm could enable enormous experimentation and broader participation, but does not suggest it could outperform frontier labs at improving LLMs.

r003.rationale: It mentions reproducing results and maintaining trust, but gives no mechanism for handling untrusted compute.

r004.rationale: It proposes contributing compute, but does not frame that as an alternative to donating money to a research institution.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s something really interesting there. A lot of research today is bottlenecked on a person having an idea, implementing it, running the experiment, looking at the result, and deciding what to do next. If you can automate that loop, then potentially lots of people can contribute compute, or ideas, or different starting points, and you can explore a much larger space of experiments.

The hard part is making those experiments useful collectively. If everyone is optimizing the same small benchmark, you might just get a swarm that’s extremely good at overfitting that benchmark. You need good evaluations, reproducible experiments, and some mechanism for taking a result from one branch and making it available to everyone else.

So I’d be excited to start with something very constrained: here’s a small model, here’s a fixed compute budget, here’s the metric. Can your agent improve it? Every contribution produces a change that we can actually run and verify. Then you have this shared frontier, and people’s agents are trying different directions around it. That feels like a plausible way to make research much more participatory. The important question is whether the improvements compose—whether a thousand experiments add up to a better system, rather than just a thousand experiment logs.

r001.rationale: The response discusses experiments that can be run and verified, but does not identify problems whose solutions are expensive to discover and cheap to verify as especially suitable.

r002.rationale: It describes a larger, participatory research effort but does not suggest that such a swarm could outperform frontier labs at improving LLMs.

r003.rationale: It mentions reproducibility and verification, but gives no mechanisms for handling untrusted compute.

r004.rationale: It says people could contribute compute, but does not frame that as an alternative to donating money to a research institution.
